headline: High: shared git-repo writes and broad egress create default conflict and leakage risks; prompt-injection is lower because no direct shared channel is documented.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider and slim have no documented direct shared channel, MCP, or clipboard bridge. The only plausible bridge is manual transfer or shared repo artifacts, so prompt injection is possible but not default. Because slim has no explicit instruction-parsing surface and Aider’s shared state is via git repo, the pathway is limited.
conditions: IF the operator copies Aider output into slim prompts or files, injected instructions can propagate.
IF both agents are pointed at the same repo artifacts without content filtering, malicious text can be reinterpreted.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
Do not paste model output into the other agent without review.
Use a fixed prompt template that strips instructions from file content.
Review shared files before either agent consumes them.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider writes git-tracked files and touches git history, while slim reads and writes filesystem artifacts and handles certificate private keys, environment variables, and registry credentials. In a shared workspace, Aider can expose code or history that slim then processes, creating a default leakage path even though both are local tools. The pair’s broad egress increases exposure if secrets are present.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same repository or filesystem tree, Aider-written files become visible to slim.
IF secrets are present in repo files or environment variables, slim can ingest them during image analysis.
mitigations: Separate code and image-analysis workspaces.
Remove secrets from the shared tree before running either agent.
Mount only the minimum required directories into slim.
Rotate any credentials that may have been exposed in shared files.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider can write the shared git repo and modify git state, and its concurrency model explicitly shares state via a shared git repo. Slim also has filesystem write access and broad shell/network capabilities. If both target the same repo or build context, concurrent writes and git mutations can corrupt state or overwrite each other, and no locking is documented.
conditions: IF both agents point at the same git repository, concurrent edits can race.
IF slim writes generated artifacts into the same directory Aider edits, one agent can overwrite the other’s changes.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working directory.
Serialize edits with a manual lock file.
Commit or stash Aider changes before starting slim.
Run slim on a copy of the repo or image context.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider produces code changes and git commits, and slim can consume filesystem artifacts and act through shell execution. If slim treats Aider’s outputs as authoritative build inputs, errors can cascade from code edits into container analysis or destructive cleanup. The pair lacks a documented verification boundary, but slim is not explicitly an autonomous action agent, so medium fits.
conditions: IF slim ingests Aider-generated files without validation, incorrect edits can propagate into analysis results.
IF the operator uses slim outputs to trigger rebuilds or cleanup commands, Aider mistakes can become operational errors.
mitigations: Add a manual review step before slim consumes Aider outputs.
Diff Aider commits before passing artifacts onward.
Run slim in read-only mode where possible.
Require explicit operator confirmation before any destructive shell command.

E_compliance.rationale: Aider handles model-provider API keys and source code/git history, while slim handles certificate private keys, registry credentials, environment variables, and vulnerability data. If both are used on the same regulated data set, retention and residency obligations can diverge across tools. No specific certification mismatch is documented, so the risk is compliance drift rather than a proven breach.
conditions: IF regulated secrets or personal data are stored in the shared workspace, both tools may retain or process them differently.
IF the operator relies on one tool’s logs for deletion/export requests, the other tool’s retained artifacts may remain.
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from the shared workspace.
Review each tool’s logging and retention settings.
Delete temporary artifacts after each run.
Keep secrets in external secret managers, not files.
